newsitem.title: JORDAN: Border shooting might fan Israeli-Jordan tensions.
newsitem.headline: Border shooting might fan Israeli-Jordan tensions.

text.p: The killing of seven Israeli schoolgirls by a Jordanian border guard on Thursday threatened to throw Israel's already troubled relations with its Arab neighbour into fresh crisis.

Jordan, swiftly condemning the attack as an isolated murder, tried to calm tension already running high after King Hussein warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this week he was pushing the Middle East "towards an abyss of bloodshed".
The king cut short a trip to Spain to return to Jordan, saying the bullets had been fired "at him and his sons and daughters".
Crown Prince Hassan, speaking to reporters near the site of the shooting, said: "I don't want to read this politically. It is an act of murder."

The shooting, which took place on Jordanian land leased to Israel under their 1994 peace treaty, was the most serious outbreak of violence along the heavily guarded border since the peace accord was signed.
Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti condemned the shooting as a "heinous crime" and pledged the soldier would be "prosecuted to the full extent of the law".

Officials said the two countries had set up a joint team to investigate the shooting. They stressed that 150,000 Israeli tourists had visited the country in safety since the former foes opened their border crossings.

"I don't think anybody, Israel or Jordan, is interested in a major problem," said one political analyst who asked not to be named. "This is an isolated incident happening in an atmosphere which is very tense."

Since the signing of the treaty King Hussein has been regarded as the Arab leader closest to Israel. Even before the treaty the two countries cooperated closely in security along their joint borders, diplomats say.

But he spoke out in a letter to Netanyahu, made public on Tuesday, in which he said the Israeli plans to build Jewish homes around Jerusalem and limit its next West Bank withdrawal to just nine percent of the land made peace in the Middle East "appear more and more like a distant elusive mirage".

After King Hussein's letter was published, Jordan television broadcast for two days running during prime time viewing a parliamentary debate in which opposition deputies called for the 1994 treaty to be abrogated.
Many Jordanians will see the king's message as prescient.

"There have been a lot of warnings that violence will take place and that tensions are rising," former Jordanian prime minister Taher al-Masri told Reuters. "This shows just how angry people are over the developments in Jerusalem and the West Bank."

Israeli Education Minister Zvulun Hammer, a supporter of the Jewish West Bank settlements, told Israel Army Radio the shooting showed that the king..."must hold his tongue so that a soldier doesn't take his words to mean more than he intended".
But Masri said both Israel and Jordan would try to dampen anger in both countries.
"Definitely they will try to overcome this. I think both sides will do something," he said.
